name: Private Market Valuation
title: Private Market Valuation
answer: Private market valuation is the practice of estimating what a company is worth when its shares do not trade on a public exchange. It covers early venture rounds, growth equity, buyouts, and the periodic marks that fund managers place on portfolio holdings. The work matters to limited partners, founders, employees holding options, and lenders, because no daily price exists to settle the question. In the AI sector the problem is sharper, since many young companies hold few hard assets and their value rests on models, data, and expected future cash flows.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Private market valuation is the practice of estimating what a company is worth when its shares do not trade on a public exchange. It covers early venture rounds, growth equity, buyouts, and the periodic marks that fund managers place on portfolio holdings. The work matters to limited partners, founders, employees holding options, and lenders, because no daily price exists to settle the question. In the AI sector the problem is sharper, since many young companies hold few hard assets and their value rests on models, data, and expected future cash flows.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Valuations run on the financial statements and cap tables that portfolio companies supply, together with comparable transaction data and market multiples. Funds keep these inputs in portfolio monitoring systems, spreadsheets, and increasingly in data platforms that pull from deal databases and public filings. This site tracks 517 company pages and 404 merger and acquisition filings, which is the kind of reference material analysts draw on when they need a comparable deal. For listed AI names, the 117 instruments with daily prices serve as a public market benchmark that private marks are often compared against.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The core methods are the market approach, which applies multiples from comparable companies or transactions, the income approach, which discounts projected cash flows, and the cost approach, which sums what has been invested. For early stage AI companies, practitioners often weight the most recent priced round, then adjust for performance against plan, sector movement, and changes in the public comparables. Option pricing models such as the Black Scholes framework are used to allocate value across share classes when preferred and common stock have different rights. Each quarter the fund documents the inputs and the reasoning behind any change in the mark.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Private marks are governed by fund valuation policies, and in the United States the fair value standard under accounting rules requires an estimate of exit price rather than a cost figure. Auditors test the assumptions, and limited partner advisory committees review the process, while regulators examine whether marks are being smoothed to flatter reported returns. Provenance matters: the source of each comparable, the date of the last financing, and the rights attached to each security all need to be traceable.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward more frequent and more standardized reporting, with data providers pushing to automate comparable selection and to shorten the lag between a market move and a revised mark. Secondary markets for fund interests and for employee shares are giving outside observers more price signals than the asset class used to have. For AI companies specifically, the open questions are how to value data sets, compute commitments, and model risk when the technology and its regulation are both moving quickly. Expect continued tension between the desire for smooth quarterly numbers and the demand for marks that reflect what a buyer would actually pay.
